issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s removal of produce from a threshing floor is prohibited only when it is done at a time or in a manner intended to prevent its due division.
material_facts: The tenant brought the harvested crop to the threshing floor for division and was prepared to divide it according to the legally prescribed shares.
The landlord insisted on a greater share and did not cooperate in division despite repeated efforts to resolve the dispute.
A revenue official measured the crop, and the tenant removed it to prevent deterioration after the landlord’s agent did not attend for division.
issues.conclusion: The tenant did not contravene the prohibition on removing produce because the removal was not intended to prevent due division.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Madras Cultivating Tenants (Payment of Fair Rent) Act, 1956 prohibits a tenant from failing to bring the crop to the threshing floor or from removing any portion at such a time or in such a manner as to prevent due division. Where the landlord does not cooperate in division, section 3(3) of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 permits the tenant to deposit the market value of rent payable in kind. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: cultivating_tenant_eviction_case and crop_brought_for_division and tenant_ready_to_divide_lawfully and landlord_obstructed_division and crop_measured_before_removal and removal_to_prevent_deterioration

predicates.cultivating_tenant_eviction_case: A landlord seeks the eviction of a cultivating tenant from a holding.
predicates.crop_brought_for_division: The tenant brings the harvested crop to the threshing floor for division.
predicates.tenant_ready_to_divide_lawfully: The tenant is prepared to divide the crop according to the legally prescribed shares.
predicates.landlord_obstructed_division: The landlord or the landlord’s agent obstructs or refuses division according to the legally prescribed shares.
predicates.crop_measured_before_removal: An official measures the crop before the tenant removes it.
predicates.removal_to_prevent_deterioration: The tenant removes the crop to prevent it from deteriorating while division is delayed.

issues.definition: When a cultivating-tenant eviction case involves a crop brought for lawful division, the tenant’s readiness to divide, the landlord’s obstruction, measurement before removal, and removal to prevent deterioration, the removal is not prohibited.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s failure to pay rent in time or deposit it as prescribed gives the landlord grounds to seek eviction, but does not require eviction and cannot alone justify refusing to consider discretionary time to pay.
material_facts: The tenant did not pay the rent within the required time or deposit its market value in court, but sent the landlord a money order for the tenant’s calculation of the landlord’s share.
The landlord had refused to cooperate in division of the crop and refused the money order.
The Revenue Divisional Officer refused to consider giving the tenant time to pay because the tenant had not made a court deposit.
The High Court set aside the eviction order after finding that the officer had misunderstood the scope of that discretion.
issues.conclusion: The landlord had grounds to apply for eviction, but the Revenue Divisional Officer was required to consider whether to give the tenant time to pay, having regard to the circumstances; failure to make a court deposit could not itself be a reason to refuse to exercise that discretion.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(2) and 3(3) of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 address rent arrears and deposit of rent payable in kind. Section 3(4)(b) gives the Revenue Divisional Officer discretion to allow time for payment, considering the relative circumstances of landlord and tenant. That discretion operates where the tenant has not made the deposit and must be exercised by considering the circumstances of the case. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.cultivating_tenant_eviction_case: A landlord seeks the eviction of a cultivating tenant from a holding.
predicates.rent_unpaid_or_undeposited: The tenant fails to pay rent in time or to deposit it, and the landlord seeks eviction on that basis.
predicates.officer_refused_time_to_pay_solely_for_n: The decision-maker refuses to consider allowing time to pay solely because the tenant did not make a deposit.

issues.definition: When a cultivating-tenant eviction case involves rent left unpaid or undeposited and the decision-maker refuses time to pay solely for that reason, the decision-maker must exercise discretion based on the circumstances of the case.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere in revision when a decision-maker fails to exercise jurisdiction because of a patent error of law, and the Supreme Court may decline to disturb that corrective order in special-leave jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Revenue Divisional Officer refused to exercise the statutory discretion to allow time for payment because the tenant had not deposited rent.
The High Court set aside the eviction order in revision.

The appeal to the Supreme Court challenged the High Court’s revisional interference, but the officer’s view of the law was patently incorrect and the officer had failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in him.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering in revision, and the Supreme Court declined to disturb its order under Article 136.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6-B of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 conferred revisional jurisdiction to the extent provided by section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A decision-maker’s failure to exercise jurisdiction on the basis of a patently incorrect view of law may justify revisional interference. Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court would not interfere with the High Court’s corrective order in these circumstances. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_revisional_ord: An appeal by special leave challenges a High Court order made in revision.
predicates.lower_decision_made_on_patent_error_of_l: The decision-maker’s order rests on a patently incorrect view of the law.
predicates.lower_authority_failed_to_exercise_juris: The decision-maker does not exercise jurisdiction vested in that office.
predicates.high_court_corrected_the_error: The High Court intervenes in revision to correct the legal error and resulting failure to exercise jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges a revisional order correcting a patent legal error that caused a lower authority to fail to exercise jurisdiction, the Supreme Court does not disturb the High Court’s order.
